openingProblem.problem: In 1972 Nixon and Brezhnev signed the first treaty limiting nuclear missiles. In 1979 the USSR invaded Afghanistan and the next arms treaty was shelved. Was détente a real change in the Cold War, or only a pause?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what did each superpower want from détente?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why détente? 1963–1972
chunks.body:
**Détente**, a French word meaning a relaxation of tension, describes the thaw in US-Soviet relations from the late 1960s to the late 1970s. Its roots lay in the fear of the early 1960s. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought nuclear fear to its peak and produced the first arms control agreement, the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963. Further progress was derailed by the American escalation in Vietnam, but the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 was a clear sign that détente was emerging.

By the late 1960s both superpowers had concrete reasons to talk. The arms race was "incredibly expensive", and both faced economic difficulties at home as resources were diverted to weapons. The Soviet Union had embarked on a massive build-up of intercontinental missiles to reach parity with the US, and in January 1967 President Johnson revealed that Moscow was building an anti-ballistic missile (ABM) defence around its capital. Such defences were dangerous because a side that could shoot down incoming missiles might be tempted to strike first. Johnson's Defence Secretary, Robert McNamara, called the cycle of action and reaction "an insane road to follow".

Each side also had strategic motives. The Sino-Soviet split made better relations with Washington more attractive to Moscow. The United States, bogged down in Vietnam, hoped that better relations with the USSR would help limit future conflicts, and Nixon wanted to give Moscow and Beijing "bigger fish to fry" than helping North Vietnam. Nixon's opening to China in 1972 changed the context of the Cold War and encouraged the move towards détente with the Soviet Union. In Europe, West Germany's *Ostpolitik* contributed: between 1970 and 1973 Bonn signed treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and Prague accepting the post-war frontiers, a four-power agreement on Berlin was reached, and the two German states signed a Basic Treaty.

Détente also reflected a choice about values. Henry Kissinger, Nixon's National Security Adviser, told the Senate in 1974 that détente "should not be made to wait upon Soviet domestic reforms": the US would deal with the USSR as it was.

This mattered because détente was built on shared interests rather than shared values, which meant that it would last only as long as those interests outweighed the rivalry.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both continued to build weapons during détente.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Moscow and Beijing kept supplying Hanoi.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ostpolitik and the China opening changed the context.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were regional moves, not superpower agreements.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The cost of the arms race was an important reason for détente, but strategic calculations mattered more.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The arms race was 'incredibly expensive' for both sides, yet Moscow was also drawn by the Sino-Soviet split and Washington by its need to limit the conflict in Vietnam.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that each side sought détente to gain a strategic advantage elsewhere, so cost made talks attractive while strategy made them urgent.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Soviet drive for nuclear parity also meant that by the late 1960s only agreement could stop an endless and dangerous build-up.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Cost was therefore a necessary condition, while strategy explains why détente came when it did.

chunks.title: Arms control: SALT I and SALT II, 1969–1979
chunks.body:
The core of détente was arms control. Formal **Strategic Arms Limitation Talks** (SALT) opened in Helsinki on 17 November 1969. For two and a half years the two sides bargained over missile defences, verification and American concern about new Soviet submarine-launched missiles. On 26 May 1972, in Moscow, President Nixon and the Soviet leader **Leonid Brezhnev** signed the **ABM Treaty** and an interim agreement capping the number of intercontinental missiles. For the first time in the Cold War, the superpowers had agreed to limit the number of nuclear missiles in their arsenals. The ABM Treaty allowed each side only 200 interceptors at two sites. The Office of the Historian calls SALT I "the crowning achievement of the Nixon-Kissinger strategy of détente".

SALT I had a major gap. It did not stop either side fitting several independently targeted warheads (MIRVs) onto a single missile, so each could still multiply its striking power. A second round, SALT II, began in late 1972 and ran through three presidencies. At Vladivostok in November 1974, President Ford and Brezhnev agreed a framework: 2,400 strategic delivery vehicles and 1,320 MIRV systems for each side. But disputes over bombers, cruise missiles and verification dragged on.

President Carter and Brezhnev finally signed **SALT II** in Vienna on 17 June 1979, limiting each side to 2,250 delivery vehicles. By then the political climate had turned. A coalition of Republicans and conservative Democrats in the Senate distrusted the treaty because of the Soviet crackdown on dissent at home, its interventions abroad and doubts about verification. When the USSR invaded Afghanistan on 25 December 1979, Carter asked the Senate not to consider the treaty, and it was never ratified. Both sides nonetheless promised to observe its terms.

Was arms control a success? It slowed the race in some areas, and it established that the superpowers could negotiate limits. But it limited numbers of launchers rather than warheads, and its fate depended on the wider political relationship.

This mattered because SALT showed both the promise and the limits of détente: agreement was possible on managing the nuclear balance, which meant that arms control survived even when the political relationship broke down.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Vladivostok framework was agreed in 1974.

chunks.title: Helsinki, 1975: who gained?
chunks.body:
Since 1954 the Soviet Union had wanted a European security conference that would formally recognise the borders drawn after the Second World War. During détente the West agreed. NATO ministers accepted the idea in December 1971, the **Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe** opened in Helsinki in July 1973, and on 1 August 1975 thirty-five states signed the **Helsinki Final Act**: every European country except Albania, plus the US and Canada.

The Act was divided into four "baskets". The first dealt with security: borders, territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes and confidence-building measures between armed forces. The second covered trade and scientific cooperation. The third concerned human rights: freedom of emigration, the reunification of divided families, cultural exchanges and freedom of the press. The fourth arranged follow-up meetings.

At first the Soviets seemed the clear winners. Tony Judt argues that Brezhnev "could not have wished for more": the post-war division of Europe was officially accepted, the sovereignty of East Germany and the other satellites was conceded, and the Western powers renounced any armed intervention. Together with West Germany's treaties of the early 1970s, Helsinki amounted to a "retrospective confirmation and acceptance of Potsdam". Some Western activists condemned the agreement for accepting the Soviet annexation of the Baltic states.

But the third basket had unexpected consequences. Most signatories treated the human rights clauses as window dressing. Yet from them, Judt writes, "was born the Helsinki Rights movement". Dissidents in the Soviet Union and across Eastern Europe formed Helsinki monitoring groups, demanding only that their governments keep the promises they had signed. Repression continued (in 1977 leaders of a Ukrainian Helsinki group were sentenced to three to fifteen years), but every arrest could now be publicised as a breach of Moscow's own commitments. The follow-up meeting in Belgrade in 1977–78 introduced a review of violations. Judt concludes that Brezhnev had "inadvertently opened a breach in their own defenses", and that it "was to prove mortal".

This mattered because the Soviets won the borders they wanted but gave their critics a weapon, which meant that Helsinki strengthened Soviet control in the short run and weakened it in the long run.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The USSR gained formal acceptance of Europe's post-war borders.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The West had never seriously threatened those borders anyway.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The third basket gave dissidents a legal basis for protest.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Signatories at first treated it as window dressing.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Helsinki's long-term effect undermined Soviet rule.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In the short run repression continued.

chunks.title: The collapse of détente, 1975–1979
chunks.body:
By the end of the 1970s détente had collapsed. The Office of the Historian identifies a basic problem: the United States and the Soviet Union "had different visions of what détente meant". Many Americans had expected it to end the Cold War, and were disillusioned when competition continued, especially in the Third World.

**Angola** was an early test. When Portugal withdrew from its colonies after the 1974 revolution, Angola's independence movements fought for power. The US aided the FNLA and UNITA, the USSR the Marxist MPLA, and Cuba sent troops to halt a South African advance. The crisis of 1974–75 helped strain US-Soviet relations.

Values returned to American policy. **Jimmy Carter**, inaugurated in January 1977, made human rights "the cornerstone" of his foreign policy, and in his first weeks his administration criticised violations in the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia. This sat uneasily beside Helsinki's promise of non-intervention in each state's internal affairs. Meanwhile the Soviet crackdown on dissent turned Senate opinion against SALT II.

The final blow came at the end of December 1979, when thousands of Soviet troops entered **Afghanistan** to save a friendly socialist regime from Islamic insurgents. It was the only time the USSR invaded a country outside the Eastern bloc. Carter responded with what became the Carter Doctrine, a pledge to protect Middle Eastern oil from Soviet power, and with sanctions, trade embargoes, a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics and more aid to the Afghan rebels. He asked the Senate to shelve SALT II, and arms control talks stopped until Gorbachev came to power.

Was détente a genuine change or a tactical pause? For the US it was a way of managing a rival while competing elsewhere; for the USSR it confirmed parity and the post-war borders. Neither side gave up the competition. Yet détente left lasting results: SALT's limits were still observed, and Helsinki gave dissidents a weapon that would matter in the 1980s.

This mattered because détente failed to change the rivalry but did change its rules, which meant that when the Cold War ended, the arms control and human rights frameworks of the 1970s were ready to be used.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both sides gained from it for several years.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Third World conflicts such as Angola undermined trust.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: These were local conflicts with their own causes.
Détente was already in trouble before the invasion.

segments.text: The cost of the arms race
Soviet ABM defences around Moscow
The ABM Treaty and interim agreement of 1972
The Vladivostok framework of 1974
SALT II signed but never ratified

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the cost of the arms race the main reason for détente between 1969 and 1975?
essayQuestions.namedFactor: the cost of the arms race

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The cost of the arms race, weighed first

modelPlan.thesis: The cost of the arms race made détente attractive to both sides, but strategic motives (the Sino-Soviet split for Moscow, Vietnam for Washington) explain why it came when it did.

arguments.claim: Cost and the danger of ABMs (named factor first).
The Sino-Soviet split and the China opening.
Vietnam and 'bigger fish to fry'.
Europe: Ostpolitik and the Soviet wish for recognised borders.

modelPlan.counter: Both sides kept modernising their arsenals during détente, which suggests cost was not decisive.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would détente have happened without the triangle with China? Probably not so quickly, so strategy explains its timing.

segments.text: The cost of the arms race was an important reason for détente, but not the main one.
The arms race was 'incredibly expensive' and both sides faced economic difficulties, yet the Sino-Soviet split drew Moscow towards the US and Vietnam drew Washington towards Moscow.
This meant that cost made agreement desirable, while strategy made it urgent, so SALT I followed the China opening in the same year.
However, the danger of Soviet ABM defences and the drive to parity meant that, by the late 1960s, only agreement could stop an endless build-up.
Cost was therefore a necessary condition of détente, but strategic calculation was its main driver.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Détente was a tactical pause rather than a genuine change in superpower relations.” Discuss with reference to the period 1969 to 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Whether détente changed the rivalry or only its rules

modelPlan.thesis: Détente did not end the rivalry, since both sides kept competing in the Third World; but it genuinely changed the rules, through arms control and Helsinki, in ways that outlasted its collapse.

arguments.claim: For: different visions and continued competition.
For: collapse after Afghanistan.
Against: the first limits on nuclear missiles.
Against: Helsinki's lasting human rights effect.

modelPlan.counter: Kissinger's view that détente need not wait on Soviet reform shows it was a pragmatic arrangement from the start.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did détente change the rules of the rivalry? Yes: arms limits were observed even after SALT II was shelved.

segments.text: Détente was more than a tactical pause, although it did not end the rivalry.
The superpowers kept competing in Angola in 1974–75 and Afghanistan in 1979, yet SALT I in 1972 was the first limit on nuclear missiles and both sides observed SALT II even unratified.
This meant that détente changed how the rivalry was managed, so arms control survived the political collapse.
However, the two sides had different visions of détente, and by 1979 cooperation had given way to renewed competition.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: détente paused the confrontation but genuinely changed its rules.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the significance of the Helsinki Final Act for superpower relations between 1975 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The significance of the Helsinki Final Act

modelPlan.thesis: In the short term Helsinki confirmed Soviet borders and was seen as a Soviet gain, but its human rights basket gave dissidents a weapon and, under Carter, became a source of US-Soviet friction.

arguments.claim: Soviet gains: borders and non-intervention.
Western criticism of the concession.
The third basket and the Helsinki groups.
Human rights and friction under Carter.

modelPlan.counter: In the short run repression continued, as the 1977 sentences show, so the impact took time.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By what criterion? Effect on the relationship: by 1979 human rights, the issue Helsinki made legitimate, was dividing the superpowers.

segments.text: Helsinki was significant because it turned human rights into an issue between the superpowers.

The Act gave the USSR 'retrospective confirmation and acceptance of Potsdam', yet its third basket inspired Helsinki monitoring groups, and Carter's administration criticised Soviet violations from 1977.
This meant that the West could challenge Soviet conduct by appealing to Moscow's own commitments, so the Act became a source of friction.
However, in 1975 it looked like a Soviet victory, and in the short run the Soviets could suppress the groups.
Helsinki's significance therefore lay less in what was agreed than in what it allowed others to demand.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons for, and the results of, the SALT negotiations between 1969 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and which result lasted

modelPlan.thesis: SALT was driven by the cost and danger of the arms race, especially Soviet parity and missile defences; it produced the first limits on nuclear weapons, but SALT II fell victim to the collapse of détente.

arguments.claim: Reason: cost and parity.
Reason: the danger of ABM defences.
Result: SALT I and the ABM Treaty.
Result: SALT II signed but never ratified.

modelPlan.counter: SALT left MIRVs uncontrolled until late in the decade, so warheads kept multiplying.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which result lasted? The habit of observing agreed limits, which both sides kept even without ratification.

segments.text: SALT was driven above all by the danger that missile defences and parity posed to deterrence.
In 1967 Johnson revealed Soviet ABM defences around Moscow, and McNamara called the action-reaction cycle 'an insane road to follow'.
This meant that both sides had a reason to cap defences and missiles, so in May 1972 they signed the ABM Treaty and the interim agreement.
However, SALT I left MIRVs uncontrolled, and SALT II, signed in June 1979, was never ratified after the invasion of Afghanistan.
SALT therefore achieved the first limits on nuclear arms, but its later success depended on the political climate.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for the collapse of détente between 1975 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Détente collapsed because the superpowers had different visions of it: continued Soviet involvement in the Third World and the US turn to human rights eroded trust, and the invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 completed the breakdown.

arguments.claim: Different visions and overblown expectations.
Angola and the Third World.
Human rights and dissent.
Afghanistan and SALT II.

modelPlan.counter: Arms control survived the collapse, since both sides observed SALT II.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The different visions, because they made every later dispute look like a betrayal.

segments.text: Détente collapsed mainly because the two superpowers had different visions of what it meant.
The US expected restraint, yet in 1974–75 the USSR backed the MPLA in Angola, and from 1977 Carter's human rights policy criticised Soviet abuses.
This meant that each side saw the other breaking the spirit of détente, so trust collapsed before the invasion of Afghanistan.
However, the invasion of December 1979 was the decisive event, since it led Carter to shelve SALT II.
Détente therefore collapsed from contradictions that Afghanistan exposed rather than created.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the aims of the United States and the Soviet Union in pursuing détente between 1969 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The aims of the two superpowers

modelPlan.thesis: Both sought to reduce the cost and danger of the arms race, but the US wanted Soviet restraint and leverage in Vietnam and against China, while the USSR wanted parity and recognition of its post-war gains.

arguments.claim: Similarity: reducing the cost and risk of the arms race.
Similarity: both used China as a factor.
Difference: Soviet aim of recognised borders.
Difference: US expectation of restraint.

modelPlan.counter: Both continued to compete in the Third World, which suggests their aims were similar: advantage without war.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? The view of competition: the US expected restraint, the USSR did not.

segments.text: Both superpowers sought to limit the arms race, but they wanted different things from détente.
Both faced an 'incredibly expensive' arms race, yet the USSR had sought recognition of its post-war borders since 1954, whereas the US hoped détente would bring restraint and help in Vietnam.
This meant that the USSR saw détente as confirming its gains, while the US saw it as a way of limiting Soviet expansion.
However, both sides kept competing, as Angola shows, so neither expected détente to end the rivalry.
The decisive difference was therefore over competition, which explains why each accused the other of betraying détente.
